summary: Describes the Selectively Reliable Multicast Protocol, a transport protocol for any-to-any multicast that mixes reliable and best-effort messages. It is meant for distributed simulation, where only the latest reliable value for each data identifier needs delivery, and the application picks which messages are reliable. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A group chat where most messages can get lost, but a few important ones must arrive. Chatter carries hints that help spot missing important ones.

subtitle: A transport protocol for multicast networks mixing reliable and best-effort messages.

tldr.problem: Distributed simulation applications need to send many frequent updates (like position data) that can tolerate loss, mixed with occasional critical updates (like appearance changes) that must arrive reliably. Flooding the network with retransmissions for all messages defeats the purpose of multicast.
tldr.mechanism: SRMP uses three transmission modes: Mode 0 for best-effort delivery (no retransmission), Mode 1 for reliable multicast using negative acknowledgements (retransmit only when a receiver detects loss), and Mode 2 for reliable unicast transactions. Best-effort messages piggyback sequence numbers of recent reliable messages, allowing receivers to detect missing reliable messages without extra overhead.
tldr.outcome: SRMP enables efficient reliable multicast in simulation environments by leveraging the mix of traffic types. However, it remains Experimental and has not seen widespread adoption beyond its original application domain.

today: RFC 4410 defines an Experimental protocol primarily designed for distributed virtual simulation environments. It has not been widely adopted outside of specialized simulation communities. The protocol's effectiveness depends on having traffic with the specific characteristics of simulation data—a high volume of best-effort state updates mixed with infrequent critical data. Applications with different traffic patterns may find other multicast protocols more suitable. However, the selective reliability concept has influenced thinking about multicast protocol design.

sections.title: Mixed-Mode Multicast Transport
sections.content:
The Selectively Reliable Multicast Protocol (SRMP) is a transport protocol designed for distributed simulation and similar applications where a multicast group sends both critical and non-critical data. The key insight is that best-effort messages can carry sequence numbers of reliable messages at almost no cost, allowing receivers to detect missing reliable data without extra acknowledgement traffic.

In a distributed virtual simulation, participants continuously broadcast low-level state updates—position, orientation, velocity—which arrive frequently and become outdated quickly. These best-effort messages can tolerate loss because newer updates will supersede them. However, some data changes—avatar appearance, object creation, event triggering—happen rarely and must be reliably received. SRMP lets the application choose which messages are reliable and which are not, then uses the high volume of best-effort traffic to efficiently convey loss information for the critical messages.
sections.plainLanguage: In a multiplayer game, your position changes constantly and gets sent many times per second—it's OK if some packets get lost because the next position update will be fresher. But if someone buys a new outfit, that must arrive reliably. SRMP uses the constant position updates to tell everyone about any missed outfit changes.

sections.title: Protocol Structure and Sublayers
sections.content:
SRMP has two functional sublayers. The Selectively Reliable Transport (SRT) layer handles the three transmission modes and manages retransmission buffers. The Bundling sublayer sits between SRT and UDP, aggregating multiple SRMP messages into bundles to improve efficiency and implementing congestion control.

The bundling layer implements TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control (TFMCC), which adapts the sender's rate based on loss rates and round-trip times reported by receivers. When the network becomes congested, senders reduce their transmission rate. Importantly, congestion control is achieved by dropping Mode 0 (best-effort) messages at the sender, leaving Mode 1 (reliable) messages intact.

Messages are encapsulated in bundles—aggregations of multiple SRMP messages destined for the same multicast address, plus a bundle header that carries DSN (Data Sequence Number) information about recent reliable messages.
sections.plainLanguage: SRMP has two layers: one that decides which messages are reliable and handles retries, and another that packs messages together, watches network congestion, and drops less-important messages when the network gets crowded.

sections.title: Three Transmission Modes
sections.content:
SRMP defines three modes of transmission for different reliability requirements. Mode 0 messages are sent best-effort with no retransmission—if lost, they are simply discarded. They carry no sequence numbers and are not acknowledged. In simulation, Mode 0 is used for rapid state updates like position.

Mode 1 messages are reliably delivered to all multicast group members using selective retransmission. Each Mode 1 message is assigned a sequence number and a data identifier (dataID). The sender buffers the most recent Mode 1 message for each dataID. Receivers detect loss by checking the DSN (sequence numbers of reliable messages) in bundle headers. When loss is detected, a receiver sends a NACK (negative acknowledgement), and the sender retransmits the buffered message. Only the latest version of each dataID is kept—if an older reliable message is lost, it will never be requested because a newer one will be in the next bundle header.

Mode 2 is for reliable unicast transactions between two members of the multicast group. Mode 2 messages are sent using unicast addressing and require a positive acknowledgement (ACK) from the recipient. This is useful for point-to-point exchanges within a multicast group.
sections.plainLanguage: Mode 0 is 'send and forget.' Mode 1 is 'I'll send this important message, and if someone says it got lost, I'll send it again.' Mode 2 is 'I need to deliver this to one person, and they must confirm they got it.'

sections.title: Message Bundling and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The bundling sublayer collects SRMP messages and packs them into bundles before transmission. Each bundle contains a header with DSN entries for each dataID for which the sender recently transmitted a Mode 1 message. The DSN carries the dataID, the latest sequence number, and the number of segments (if the message was fragmented).

Bundling improves efficiency by reducing per-message overhead and allows congestion control. When network congestion is detected through TFMCC feedback, the sender reduces its transmission rate by randomly dropping Mode 0 messages. Mode 1 messages are never dropped to preserve reliability.

TFMCC (TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control) works by having each receiver measure its loss rate and round-trip time to the sender, then calculate a desired sending rate using an equation that models TCP's congestion behavior. Receivers send feedback reports to the sender. Through a suppression mechanism, only a subset of receivers provide feedback to avoid overwhelming the sender with acknowledgements. The sender selects the receiver with the lowest reported rate as the limiting receiver and adjusts its transmission rate accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are bundled together for efficiency. When the network gets congested, the sender slows down by skipping some less-important (Mode 0) messages, using feedback from receivers about packet loss to decide how fast it can safely send.

sections.title: Loss Detection and Recovery
sections.content:
Mode 1 loss is detected by examining DSN entries in bundle headers. A receiver expects Mode 1 messages to arrive with monotonically increasing sequence numbers (modulo 512). If the DSN shows a sequence number higher than expected for a dataID, the receiver knows a message was lost and sends a NACK.

To avoid an ACK implosion (where many receivers simultaneously send NACKs, overwhelming the sender), SRMP uses NACK suppression. NACKs are held in a buffer and sent only within a time window during the next outgoing bundle transmission. If another receiver sends a NACK for the same missing message, the other receivers suppress their redundant NACKs. The suppression window is based on the bundle timeout, which is configurable (minimum 1 ms, recommended 10 ms).

For Mode 2 messages, the receiver sends an explicit ACK, and the sender retransmits if the ACK is not received within a timeout. Because Mode 2 is used for individual transactions, the small number of ACKs is not a concern.

The protocol also includes a heartbeat mechanism where senders can optionally transmit empty bundles periodically to trigger loss detection, ensuring that missing reliable messages are detected even in quiet periods.
sections.plainLanguage: When a receiver notices a Mode 1 message is missing, it sends back a request to resend it. To avoid everyone asking at once, receivers hold their requests briefly and let other receivers' requests suppress duplicates. For Mode 2 transactions, the recipient just confirms 'I got it.'
